title: Mathurā
summary: The holy city where Lord Kṛṣṇa appeared in the prison of Kaṁsa.
body:
Mathurā is one of the oldest holy cities of India, on the bank of the Yamunā. In the Bhāgavatam it is the capital of the Yadu dynasty, ruled in that period by the tyrant Kaṁsa.

It was in Kaṁsa's prison here that Kṛṣṇa appeared to Devakī and Vasudeva. Years later Kṛṣṇa returned from Vraja to Mathurā and ended Kaṁsa's rule.

Listed in a Vraja pastime-places catalogue as: Great Forests (Adhivanas). Source: https://vanachari.blogspot.com/2023/12/pastime-places.html
source_ref: Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 10.3; 10.43–10.44; https://vanachari.blogspot.com/2023/12/pastime-places.html

title: Vṛndāvana
summary: The forest of Vraja on the Yamunā where Kṛṣṇa spent his childhood with the cowherd boys and the cows.
body:
Vṛndāvana is the principal dhāma of Kṛṣṇa's pastimes, which the accounts describe as spread over sixteen krośas among the twelve principal forests of Bhauma Vṛndāvana. Rādhā-Govinda are depicted seated on a jewelled throne under a desire tree there, served by Their intimate associates. When Rādhā vanished during a pastime, Kṛṣṇa searched the groves and pleasure gardens along the Yamunā for her.

Vṛndāvana is part of the pastoral land of Vraja. It is described as a place of beautiful forests, the Yamunā, hills and meadows, full of birds, peacocks and cows.

The Bhāgavatam describes the residents of Vraja moving there, and here Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma grazed the cows with their friends and performed many of the pastimes that are remembered by devotees to this day.

title: Govardhana Hill
summary: The sacred hill in Vraja that Kṛṣṇa lifted to protect the residents from Indra's storm.
body:
Govardhana is a hill in Vraja that provided grass and water for the cows of the cowherd community. It is regarded by devotees as non-different from the Lord.

Its best-known story is the one in which Kṛṣṇa held it up like an umbrella to shelter the people of Vraja from a devastating rain.

title: Madhuvana
summary: The forest on the Yamunā where young Dhruva practised austerity and saw the Lord.
body:
Madhuvana is one of the twelve main forests of Vṛndāvana, once the home of the demon Madhu, and it was named after Maholī, the ancient capital of Madhuvana and original site of Mathurā. Here Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma played with the cowherd boys, drank honey at Madhu-kuṇḍa, and sported in its groves. The account also recounts a butter-theft episode in which Yaśodā admitted Kṛṣṇa could not have stolen the butter because He was in Madhuvana, and it describes Mahārāja Ambarīṣa's austerities in the forest.

Madhuvana is a forest on the bank of the Yamunā. Nārada instructed Dhruva to go there to practise his worship.

Dhruva stayed there, steadily increasing his austerity, until the Lord appeared before him.

title: Kurukṣetra
summary: The field where the Bhagavad-gītā was spoken between two armies.
body:
Kurukṣetra is an ancient field of sacrifice and pilgrimage. It is best known as the site of the great war between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas.

Just before the fighting began, Kṛṣṇa, acting as Arjuna's charioteer, spoke the Bhagavad-gītā here.
source_ref: Bhagavad-gītā 1.1

title: Tālavana
summary: The second forest on Vraja’s parikrama path, full of date-palm trees and known for a beautiful clear lake filled with blue lotuses.
body:
The second forest on Vraja’s parikrama path, full of date-palm trees and known for a beautiful clear lake filled with blue lotuses, whose water fulfils all desires. In New Vraja-dhāma, Madhuvana and Tālavana rest on a gently rolling pasture where Śyāmasundara’s cows graze. Dhenuka, the donkey demon, was killed by Balarāma here, and afterwards the gopas refused the contaminated fruit. Caitanya Mahāprabhu visited Tālavana, worshipped Balarāma and bathed in Vetra-gaṅgā.

title: Kumudavana
summary: Kumudavana is one of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, full of kumuda lotuses and known also as Kondaliyā, where Kṛṣṇa quarrelled with Śrīdāmā.
body:
Kumudavana is one of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, full of kumuda lotuses and known also as Kondaliyā, where Kṛṣṇa quarrelled with Śrīdāmā, Subala and the gopas. Scripture describes the Yamunā once flowing through it in a winding course. Caitanya Mahāprabhu visited this small forest, and tradition says devotees who come humbly will be successful in their endeavours, especially in reaching the supreme goal. One night in Vaiśākha Kṛṣṇa brought the gopīs here for a rāsa dance.

title: Bahulavana
summary: Bahulāvana is one of the twelve forests of Vraja, and it contains Rādhā-kuṇḍa and Śyāma-kuṇḍa in Bhauma Vṛndāvana.
body:
Bahulāvana is one of the twelve forests of Vraja, and it contains Rādhā-kuṇḍa and Śyāma-kuṇḍa in Bhauma Vṛndāvana. Caitanya Mahāprabhu visited, and the residents thought the sannyāsī was a fair-complexioned Śrī Kṛṣṇa as He smiled at them and chanted Kṛṣṇa's names. Within the forest are Saṅkarṣaṇa-kuṇḍa and Kṛṣṇa-kuṇḍa, and bathing in them during Caitra lets one see the forms of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa who eternally reside there. Tradition quotes Śrīla Prabhupāda suggesting that the hills of New Vṛndāvana could be renamed after Govardhana.

title: Kāmyavana
summary: Kāmyavana is the fourth of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, known as the forest that fulfils all desires.
body:
Kāmyavana is the fourth of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, known as the forest that fulfils all desires, and tradition says it is extolled for its own unique places. The forest includes Kāma-sarovara and Kāmanā-kuṇḍa, and Kṛṣṇa played His flute from Candrasena Hill here, so that the girls of Vraja fainted. Kṛṣṇa and His friends once became so absorbed in play at Āṭora that twenty-four hours passed without their noticing.

A sacred forest of Vraja, listed among the twelve forests.

title: Khadiravana
summary: Khadiravana is one of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, named for its khadira (acacia) trees.
body:
Khadiravana is one of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, named for its khadira (acacia) trees, where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa are eternally absorbed in transcendental exchanges. Merely visiting it can take one to Viṣṇuloka. Caitanya Mahāprabhu came here chanting in ecstatic love while His guide Kṛṣṇadāsa narrated Kṛṣṇa's pastimes there, and Lokanātha and Bhūgarbha Gosvāmīs performed bhajana here.

title: Bhadravana
summary: Bhadravana is Lord Balarāma's favourite forest and is named after Him, Balabhadra, and it is one of the twelve forests of Vraja.
body:
Bhadravana is Lord Balarāma's favourite forest and is named after Him, Balabhadra, and it is one of the twelve forests of Vraja. Rūpa Gosvāmī completed Lalita-mādhava on the bank of Bhadra-sarovara in this forest, and tradition says reading or hearing such accounts here is especially fitting. Sudāmā, one of Kṛṣṇa's gopa friends, prefers Bhadravana for frolicking with Kṛṣṇa. Vaikuṇṭha-pura, where Kṛṣṇa revealed the unlimited expanse of Vaikuṇṭha at His friends' request, lies in its southeastern corner.

title: Bhāṇḍīravana
summary: Bhāṇḍīravana is the forest named after the famous banyan Bhāṇḍīraka, also called Akṣaya-vaṭa, and it is listed among the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana.
body:
Bhāṇḍīravana is the forest named after the famous banyan Bhāṇḍīraka, also called Akṣaya-vaṭa, and it is listed among the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana. Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa were married here beneath the banyan, and the same name also belongs to a forest where Balarāma killed Pralambāsura, for which Indra gave Him the names Baladeva and Pralambaghna. Tradition recounts Rati-mañjarī bringing a picture of Kṛṣṇa to Rādhā while She sat in this forest, and Nārada Muni hearing two parrots debate the Vedānta-sūtra here. Hearing or reciting the account of the wedding beneath this banyan is said to free one from the effects of past sins.

title: Bilvavana
summary: Bilvavana is one of the twelve great forests of Vṛndāvana, on the western side of the Yamunā.
body:
Bilvavana is one of the twelve great forests of Vṛndāvana, on the western side of the Yamunā, and tradition says that passing through it on parikrama is equal to visiting the major holy places. The principal pastime described is that the goddess of fortune, Lakṣmī, performed austerities here hoping to be reborn as a gopī of Vraja, and she continues to do so invisibly, while a deity of her is worshipped here, which is why the forest is also called Śrīvana. This pastime shows the gopīs' unique standing as objects of Kṛṣṇa's favour, which Uddhava recognised during his visit to Vṛndāvana. The gopas also enjoyed the forest's fruits, using the hard-shelled ones as balls.

A sacred forest of Vraja, listed among the twelve forests.

Group: east of Yamunā.

title: Lohavana
summary: Lohavana is one of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, where the demon Loha once lived.
body:
Lohavana is one of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, where the demon Loha once lived. After Kaṁsa was killed, his father-in-law Jarāsandha marched on Mathurā, camped at Lohavana, and surrounded the city. Kṛṣṇa devised a plan to destroy Jarāsandha's armies while sparing Jarāsandha himself. Tradition also mentions Ayore and Gauravāi on the perimeter, connected with Kṛṣṇa's return to Vṛndāvana, and alludes to the pastime of Kṛṣṇa as a boatman on the Yamunā.

A sacred forest of Vraja, listed among the twelve forests.

title: Mahāvana
summary: Mahāvana is the first of the twelve main forests of Vṛndāvana, where Kṛṣṇa takes His birth.
body:
Mahāvana is the first of the twelve main forests of Vṛndāvana, where Kṛṣṇa takes His birth. Once the cowherd men set up camp at Chaṭīkarā and formed a semicircular boundary with their carts, and Mahāvana was abandoned afterward. The account also describes Kṛṣṇa revealing the entire universe within His body to the sage Durvāsā Muni, who had taken up residence near Rāval on the opposite side of Mahāvana from Gokula.

title: Rādhā-kuṇḍa
summary: Rādhā-kuṇḍa is one of the most frequently discussed holy places in devotional accounts, the lake of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa's intimate pastimes.
body:
Rādhā-kuṇḍa is one of the most frequently discussed holy places in devotional accounts, the lake of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa's intimate pastimes. Rūpa and Sanātana Gosvāmī built a temple of Rādhā-Madana-mohana beside it, and it is called their area a hidden, or gupta, Vṛndāvana. The temple courtyard, its two ponds, the terraces, and the inner petals of the Yoga-pīṭha are together called Rādhā-kuṇḍa, and Rāmeśvara Mahādeva guards its rear entrance. Tradition describes Rūpa Gosvāmī visiting the lake many times and sitting under the Imlī-talā tamarind tree to chant Hare Kṛṣṇa while gazing at its waves.

title: Nanda-grāma
summary: A village in Vraja connected with Kṛṣṇa's family and pastimes.
body:
The village (grāma) of Nanda Mahārāja, renamed from Nandīśvara when Nanda moved back there from Chaṭīkarā after Kṛṣṇa was seven, since it was his capital. Devotional accounts describe the view from Nandīśvara Hill, where Kṛṣṇa's pranks can be recalled, and the route Uddhava travelled from Mathurā to Nandagrāma with Kṛṣṇa's messages for the Vraja-vāsīs. Prefatory notes uses Nandagrāma heavily as a reference point for parikrama and for New Vraja-dhāma.

title: Kesi-ghata
summary: Keśī-ghāṭa is the bathing place on the Yamunā near the kadamba tree where Kṛṣṇa killed the demon Keśī.
body:
Keśī-ghāṭa is the bathing place on the Yamunā near the kadamba tree where Kṛṣṇa killed the demon Keśī. Bathing there is more sacred than bathing in the Ganges, and bathing at Viśrāma-tīrtha, also called Ādi-varāha-tīrtha, is a hundred times more sacred still. Vajranābha established a temple here with Deities of Yamunā and Yamarāja, and it is visited by throngs of brothers and sisters on Bhrātṛ-dvitīyā.

title: Seva-kunja
summary: Sevā-kuñja is a grove where the wives of Abhimanyu's clan, on their way to Kuśasthalī.
body:
Sevā-kuñja is a grove where the wives of Abhimanyu's clan, on their way to Kuśasthalī, came upon Kṛṣṇa standing by the road with only His flute for company. Jīva Gosvāmī first worshipped the Deity of Dāmodara, which Rūpa Gosvāmī had carved and offered in 1542, in a grove of Sevā-kuñja. After Sanātana Gosvāmī passed away, Jīva bought the entire area for thirty-two rupees to secure permanent worship. It is warned that an unqualified person who spends the night in Sevā-kuñja may die or go insane, though devotees in New Vraja-dhāma need not fear this.

title: Sri Radha-Damodara Temple
summary: Vṛndāvana temple of Śrī Rādhā-Dāmodara, associated with Jīva Gosvāmī and the writing of Caitanya-caritāmṛta.
body:
Deity: Śrī Rādhā-Dāmodara. Jīva Gosvāmī is named as the main Gosvāmī connected with this temple. Rūpa Gosvāmī, his uncle, was his dīkṣā-guru. Jīva is considered the principal systematizer of Gauḍīya theology.

Lineage: Madhva → Mādhavendra Purī → Īśvara Purī → Śrī Caitanya → Rūpa Gosvāmī → Jīva Gosvāmī.

Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja Gosvāmī lived and wrote at Rādhā-Dāmodara. He is famous for composing Caitanya-caritāmṛta, which he wrote in advanced age, systematizing the theology of Rūpa and Raghunātha.

Kṛṣṇadāsa's dīkṣā-guru and śikṣā-guru were Raghunātha Dāsa Gosvāmī. He also drew inspiration from Svarūpa Dāmodara through preserved notes. His lineage is given as Madhva → Mādhavendra Purī → Īśvara Purī → Śrī Caitanya → Raghunātha dāsa Gosvāmī → Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja.

Region: Vṛndāvana. Listed in the Kartika-vrata itinerary for 27 Oct.

title: Akrura-ghata
summary: Akrūra-ghāṭa is a bathing place on the Yamunā in Mathurā, also known as Brahma-hrada.
body:
Akrūra-ghāṭa is a bathing place on the Yamunā in Mathurā, also known as Brahma-hrada, where Kṛṣṇa invited the elders and gopas of Nandagrāma to see Vaikuṇṭha on the full-moon day of Kārttika. The Vraja-vāsīs entered the water there and perceived the all-pervasive brahmajyoti, but they felt unhappy without the taste of prema. Caitanya Mahāprabhu went to bathe at nearby places each day and returned here for His meals. An old account also recounts a Varāha Purāṇa narration on the benefits of bathing at this ghāṭa.

title: Mana-sarovara
summary: Tradition distinguishes Manaḥ-sarovara, a lake in the Himalayas born from Brahmā's mind (manaḥ), from the Vraja lake Māna-sarovara, which people often confuse with it.
body:
A lake in Vraja created from Rādhā's tears of proud anger (māna) during a rāsa dance on a sandy shoal of the Yamunā, and bathing there is said to give a love like Hers. Kṛṣṇa called it a lake born of Her tears and just like His heart, while Rādhā said it was her heart, so it is also called Hṛdaya-sarovara. The Yamunā flows between this lake and Vṛndāvana, and tradition notes it should not be confused with Manaḥ-sarovara in the Himalayas.

Tradition distinguishes Manaḥ-sarovara, a lake in the Himalayas born from Brahmā's mind (manaḥ), from the Vraja lake Māna-sarovara, which people often confuse with it. Māna-sarovara was created by Rādhā's tears of proud anger (māna) when she felt slighted during a rāsa dance on a sandy shoal of the Yamunā. Here the mention is mainly for clarification, not a pastime of its own.

title: Vamsivat
summary: A banyan tree on the bank of the Yamunā, where Śrī Gopīnātha stands and calls the gopīs with His flute.
body:
A banyan tree on the bank of the Yamunā, where Śrī Gopīnātha stands and calls the gopīs with His flute, originating the mellow of the rāsa dance. Paramānanda Bhaṭṭa and Madhu Paṇḍita are connected with the Deity of Gopīnātha found here, and a temple was later built just behind the tree. The gopīs in their madness asked the banyan tree, and then other trees and creatures, where Kṛṣṇa was, and the gopīs worshipped Gopīśvara here for their own desires.

title: Nidhuvana
summary: A forest where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa meet at night, and where, in Kārttika, They wandered during the rāsa dance described in the Bhāgavatam.
body:
A forest where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa meet at night, and where, in Kārttika, They wandered during the rāsa dance described in the Bhāgavatam. When They feel tired They rest in a secluded grove, where the jewelled pavilion Raṅg-mahal is found. New Vraja-dhāma has a pavilion, and Bhauma Vṛndāvana a temple, commemorating that place, and Gopāla Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī worshipped śālagrāma-śilās in a hut near Nidhuvana.

title: Sri Radha-Gokulananda Temple
summary: Vṛndāvana temple of Rādhā-Gokulānanda, connected with Lokanātha Gosvāmī, Bhūgarbha Gosvāmī and Narottama Dāsa Ṭhākura.
body:
Deities: several, including Vijaya Govinda and Rādhā-Vinoda. Lokanātha Gosvāmī is the Gosvāmī connected with this temple.

Dīkṣā-guru: Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu, traditionally accepted. Narottama Dāsa Ṭhākura is named as Lokanātha's famous disciple.

Lineage: Madhva → Mādhavendra Purī → Īśvara Purī → Śrī Caitanya → Lokanātha Gosvāmī.

Bhūgarbha Gosvāmī was a close associate of Lokanātha. He assisted in discovering holy places in Vṛndāvana, lived in deep renunciation, and helped establish early Vraja bhajana sites. His dīkṣā-guru is traditionally accepted as Śrī Caitanya, with the lineage Madhva → Mādhavendra Purī → Īśvara Purī → Śrī Caitanya → Bhūgarbha Gosvāmī.

title: Brahmanda-ghata
summary: Brahmāṇḍa-ghāṭa is the place where Kṛṣṇa revealed the whole universe (brahmāṇḍa) within His lotus mouth to Mother Yaśodā.
body:
Brahmāṇḍa-ghāṭa is the place where Kṛṣṇa revealed the whole universe (brahmāṇḍa) within His lotus mouth to Mother Yaśodā, and because He ate mud (mṛttikā) here He is known as Mṛttikābihārī. Kavi-karṇapūra explains that Kṛṣṇa ate the dust of Vraja to glorify it as fully transcendental and worshipable. Caitanya Mahāprabhu sat on the steps here in ecstasy remembering the exchanges between Kṛṣṇa and Yaśodā, and Śrīla Prabhupāda bathed here during a 1971 parikrama. Nearby Cintāharaṇa-ghāṭa, with its deity of Lord Śiva, marks where Śiva freed Yaśodā from her anxiety.

title: Brahma-kunda
summary: Brahma-kuṇḍa lies halfway between the Harideva temple and Mānasa-gaṅgā.
body:
Brahma-kuṇḍa lies halfway between the Harideva temple and Mānasa-gaṅgā, and it was created from the water Brahmā used to bathe Kṛṣṇa after he had stolen the gopas and calves to atone for that offence. Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu visited the place after seeing Harideva and bathed there while His servant cooked lunch. Rūpa Gosvāmī discovered Vṛndā-devī here, and tradition says she still resides in Govindajī's temple at Kāman because she will not leave Vraja. Tradition says that the aśoka tree beside the lake blooms on Śukla-dvādaśī of Vaiśākha, and Bilvamaṅgala Ṭhākura, who composed Kṛṣṇa-karṇāmṛta, lived here.

title: Khelanvana
summary: Khelanavana is the forest along the Yamunā from Ūjānī to Gopī-ghāṭa, also called Khelā-tīrtha.
body:
Khelanavana is the forest along the Yamunā from Ūjānī to Gopī-ghāṭa, also called Khelā-tīrtha, where Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma are often lost in play with Their friends. Tradition describes Kīlāla-kuṇḍa here, where Kṛṣṇa splashes with the gopīs and plays ball with the gopas. Nanda Mahārāja's clan encamped at Derāvali, and the caravan of the Vraja-vāsīs' carts stretched all the way to Khelanavana during their exodus from Chaṭīkarā.

title: Rama-ghata
summary: Rāma-ghāṭa is a sacred deep bend in the Yamunā.
body:
Rāma-ghāṭa is a sacred deep bend in the Yamunā, where divinely intoxicated Balarāma taught the river a lesson in surrender by ploughing many irrigation ditches to supply water to Vṛndāvana. East of it, in a meadow around a banyan tree, Balarāma enjoyed the rāsa dance with the gopīs, and purified souls can still hear them glorifying their Lord. When Lord Nityānanda visited, absorbed in Balarāma's mood, He played with the cowherd boys and called loudly for vāruṇī and the Yamunā, so that the locals thought He was Balarāma. The place is also listed among the twenty-four bathing places (ghāṭas).

title: Viharavana
summary: Vihāravana is a secluded, flower-filled forest east of Pe, where Kṛṣṇa met Śrīmatī Rādhārāṇī while the gopas herded the cows nearby.
body:
Vihāravana is a secluded, flower-filled forest east of Pe, where Kṛṣṇa met Śrīmatī Rādhārāṇī while the gopas herded the cows nearby. The name is explained by the pleasurable exchanges (vihāra) that took place there. Lord Nityānanda stayed here during His visit to Vṛndāvana and remembered His pastimes as Balarāma, and the forest is also linked to Kṛṣṇa's flute-song that drew Rādhā and the gopīs to it.

title: Cira-ghata
summary: Cīra-ghāṭa is a golden whirlpool at a secluded place where the Yamunā first widens.
body:
Cīra-ghāṭa is a golden whirlpool at a secluded place where the Yamunā first widens, and it is where Kṛṣṇa stole the gopīs' garments while they bathed after dancing with Him. In Syāraha village, a different Cīra-ghāṭa marks the place where the unmarried gopīs performed the Kātyāyanī vow in winter, hoping to win Kṛṣṇa as their husband. Tradition says that Caitanya Mahāprabhu bathed at a Cīra-ghāṭa before resting at Teṅtulī-talā, and a second Cīra-ghāṭa near Imlī-talā is associated with another pastime.

title: Vatsavana
summary: A forest on the edge of Govardhana Hill.
body:
A forest on the edge of Govardhana Hill, where Kṛṣṇa and the cowherd boys herded their calves about a year after Brahmā had kidnapped the real boys and calves. The cows, seeing their calves from the top of Govardhana, galloped down the hill to them. The account also notes that this Vatsavana is different from another of the same name on the south end of the Yamunā, where Brahmā stole the boys and calves.

title: Candra-sarovara
summary: Candra-sarovara is the lake where Kṛṣṇa performed His spring rāsa dance with the nitya-siddha gopīs, and devotees look towards it with reverence.
body:
Candra-sarovara is the lake where Kṛṣṇa performed His spring rāsa dance with the nitya-siddha gopīs, and devotees look towards it with reverence. After the rāsa dance at this lake, Kṛṣṇa led the gopīs to Tālavana while the milkmaids sang His glories. Tradition recounts that Balarāma, resting on Govardhana Hill, crouched to watch this rāsa dance from a distance, rarely getting the chance to see it.

title: Govinda kunda
summary: Govinda-kuṇḍa is a large lake on Govardhana Hill, closely linked with the Yoga-pīṭha of Govindajī.
body:
Govinda-kuṇḍa is a large lake on Govardhana Hill, closely linked with the Yoga-pīṭha of Govindajī, where Rūpa and Sanātana Gosvāmī bathed and prayed for Govindajī's mercy. A bath there gives the benefit of one hundred fire sacrifices, which is why Vasudeva chose the spot for Bhāguri's mantras, and its water is whitish, at times even tasting like milk, unlike the blackish Yamunā. When the buried Gopāla Deity was recovered, Mādhavendra Purī began His bathing with water from Govinda-kuṇḍa on the hilltop.

summary: Kusuma-sarovara is a lake in New Vraja-dhāma, near the centre of Puṣpavana, that it is called the heartbeat of Giri Govardhana.
body:
Kusuma-sarovara is a lake in New Vraja-dhāma, near the centre of Puṣpavana, that it is called the heartbeat of Giri Govardhana. Devotional accounts describe Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa on its banks, where Rādhā praised Kṛṣṇa for decorating her, saying He had outdone even her dearest friends. A temple of Rādhā-Vanabihārī, whose Deities were stolen, depicted Kṛṣṇa combing Rādhārāṇī's hair. The lake is also linked to Rādhā and her friends stopping at Puṣpavana to collect flowers on their way to Sūrya-kuṇḍa, and to Parīkṣit Mahārāja's kīrtana with the queens.

title: Vimala-kunda
summary: Vimala-kuṇḍa is the largest and most impressive lake in Kāmyavana, and it is the starting place of Kāmyavana's parikrama.
body:
Vimala-kuṇḍa is the largest and most impressive lake in Kāmyavana, and it is the starting place of Kāmyavana's parikrama. Bathing there without offence is said to free one from sinful reactions and enable a return to Kṛṣṇa's abode at death. Tradition tells that the perspiration of Kṛṣṇa's queens during the rāsa-like pastime became this lake, and Durvāsā Muni left his disciples there before the Pāṇḍavas' meal.

title: Narada-kunda
summary: A lake in a secluded grove behind Kāmanā-kuṇḍa, where Nārada Muni fell into an ecstatic swoon while singing of Kṛṣṇa's pastimes.
body:
A lake in a secluded grove behind Kāmanā-kuṇḍa, where Nārada Muni fell into an ecstatic swoon while singing of Kṛṣṇa's pastimes, and his tears formed the pond. Nārada later composed his bhakti-sūtras here, after Kṛṣṇa asked him to stay and write them. The account also notes that a Deity of Nara-Nārāyaṇa Ṛṣi was thrown into this lake by Buddhists and recovered by Śaṅkarācārya.

title: Pavana-sarovara
summary: Pāvana-sarovara is the foremost lake of Nandagrāma, where Lord Caitanya bathed, and where pilgrims first bathe before visiting Nanda-bhavana.
body:
Pāvana-sarovara is the foremost lake of Nandagrāma, where Lord Caitanya bathed, and where pilgrims first bathe before visiting Nanda-bhavana. Kṛṣṇa would ask to be excused from the afternoon milking, saying He wanted to swim here, so He could meet the gopīs who came to fetch water among the secret groves. Rādhikā would watch Kṛṣṇa milking the cows from a watchtower by the lake, and Sanātana Gosvāmī later lived on its southeastern side.

title: Nanda-bhavana
summary: The palace of Nanda Mahārāja, which the account describes as the most prominent feature of Gokula and as the capital residence at Nandagrāma.
body:
The palace of Nanda Mahārāja, which the account describes as the most prominent feature of Gokula and as the capital residence at Nandagrāma. Rūpa Gosvāmī says it was white and calls it Āmodavardhana, and Rādhā came from Yāvaṭā each morning to cook for Kṛṣṇa here. Akrūra was brought to Nanda-bhavana, where his exchange with Kṛṣṇa's parents led to Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma's journey to Mathurā.

title: Lalita-kunda
summary: Lalitā-kuṇḍa is Lalitā-devī's lake, on the far side of the road from Nandīśvara Hill in Nandagrāma.
body:
Lalitā-kuṇḍa is Lalitā-devī's lake, on the far side of the road from Nandīśvara Hill in Nandagrāma. Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa regularly met in a secluded grove of perpetually flowering vines beside it. Vīracandra Gosvāmī was overjoyed to hear how Lalitā arranged the divine couple's meeting on Kṛṣṇa's birthday. Tradition also says that after the bull-demon was killed, Rādhā insisted Kṛṣṇa bathe in every holy place, and He bathed in Lalitā's lake, teaching that no one, not even Kṛṣṇa, can approach Rādhā without Lalitā's blessings.

title: Prema-sarovara
summary: Prema-sarovara is an octagonal lake at the heart of Premavana, filled with a rare and confidential form of transcendental love.
body:
Prema-sarovara is an octagonal lake at the heart of Premavana, filled with a rare and confidential form of transcendental love, with a temple of Prema-bihārī, a platform commemorating the rāsa dance and a swing on its banks. Once, while Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa were absorbed in loving pastimes with the gopīs, a bumblebee entered the grove after the doorkeeper Madhumaṅgala had dozed off, and the episode shows the symptoms of prema-vaicittya. Tradition says that the thoughts stirred here strengthened Kṛṣṇa's decision to leave Vraja for Mathurā, which matured when He accepted Kaṁsa's invitation.

title: Gahvaravana
summary: This dense, conch-shaped forest covers the western side of Varṣāṇā, including Dāna-, Māna- and Mora-gaṛhs, and the account compares it to the mysterious Vedas.
body:
This dense, conch-shaped forest covers the western side of Varṣāṇā, including Dāna-, Māna- and Mora-gaṛhs, and the account compares it to the mysterious Vedas. It is one of the places of toll pastimes (Dāna-līlās) in Varṣāṇā, and it leads to Gahvara-kuṇḍa, where the boys roasted chickpeas. In its northern corner stands a temple of goddess Kālī called Kātyāyanī-pīṭha, or Bhadrakālī-tīrtha, which dates back to Purāṇic times.

title: Suryakunda
summary: A lake and place of worship where Rādhā would perform Her pūjā to the sun god on Gopāṣṭamī.
body:
A lake and place of worship where Rādhā would perform Her pūjā to the sun god on Gopāṣṭamī, though Jaṭilā once forbade Her to go there. Kṛṣṇa and the gopīs once took refuge at Sūrya-kuṇḍa, where they disguised Kṛṣṇa as a brāhmaṇa boy helping to worship the sun god before Jaṭilā arrived. Later, Ṭhākura Bhaktivinoda visited Jagannātha Dāsa Bābājī here, whom he accepted as his śikṣā-guru.

title: Kokilavana
summary: Kokilavana is one of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, where the cuckoos' calls drew Rādhā and Her friends.
body:
Kokilavana is one of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, where the cuckoos' calls drew Rādhā and Her friends. Devotional accounts describe Kṛṣṇa whispering to Rādhā to come with Him to a dense forest so they could be alone, and the gopīs following His footprints until they heard the couple's voices. Rādhikā hurried there with Her closest friends on a plan proposed by Viśākhā, and for the gopīs walking into the forest was like standing beneath a thundering waterfall.

title: Apsarāvana
summary: A sub-forests (upavanas) place in Vraja listed in a Vraja pastime-places catalogue.
body:
Apsarāvana is one of the twelve sub-forests (upavanas) associated with Govardhana, and it is said to be surcharged with prema because of the water of Apsarā-kuṇḍa and Navāla-kuṇḍa. Bathing without offence in these two lakes fills a person with ecstatic love, and the trees, creepers, animals, and birds of the forest have also become filled with prema. In one pastime, Kṛṣṇa took the form of a varāha, or boar, to playfully frighten His friends, who fell down and offered prayers until the Lord revealed Himself and serenity returned. The forest's potency is said to resemble that of Premavana.

title: Kadambavana
summary: A sub-forests (upavanas) place in Vraja listed in a Vraja pastime-places catalogue.
body:
Kadambavana is a forest of kadamba trees stretching from the edge of Sutalavana to Uddhava-kuṇḍa, where Kṛṣṇa and the gopas wander after their daily wrestling match to admire forest animals and birds. Between Maṇikandalī and Yatipura are four lakes marking pastime places: Indra-kuṇḍa, Airāvata-kuṇḍa, Surabhi-kuṇḍa and Rudra-kuṇḍa. The account also describes a pastime in which Rādhā, even after relief at His return, neglected Kṛṣṇa and refused His embrace and pleas, and the account says that remembering such pastimes frees devotees from the poison of passion.

summary: A sub-forests (upavanas) place in Vraja listed in a Vraja pastime-places catalogue.
body:
Mayūravana, or Mayūra, adjoins the village of Datihā, which Vajranābha founded after Kṛṣṇa killed Dantavakra on the road to Dvārakā. Kṛṣṇa secretly met the gopīs here, and He and Śrī Rādhā sat in a grove exchanging smiles while the gopīs served them. Prompted by the peacocks' glances and the gopīs' cheers, Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa danced like peacocks, while deer, birds, and rabbits watched.

title: Nandavana
summary: A ancillary forests (prativanas) place in Vraja listed in a Vraja pastime-places catalogue.
body:
A forest in New Vraja-dhāma, listed among the adhivanas and the prativanas, where Nanda Mahārāja came to absorb himself in bhajana. Burdened by his subjects and cows, he had little time for it, so he absorbed himself in Kṛṣṇa's childhood, boyhood and youth, chanting Kṛṣṇa's names in place of his dīkṣā-mantra. Merely seeing Nandavana relieves the heart of the burning pangs of lust.

Listed in a Vraja pastime-places catalogue as: Ancillary Forests (Prativanas) (Nanda-grāma). Source: https://vanachari.blogspot.com/2023/12/pastime-places.html

title: Caraṇa-kuṇḍa
summary: A footprints of kṛṣṇa place in Vraja listed in a Vraja pastime-places catalogue.
body:
Caraṇa-kuṇḍa is the name of several lakes that are blessed by Kṛṣṇa's feet. One is in Pramodavana, where the gopīs' moods of separation are recalled, and another is near Rādhā-Govinda's temple in Kāmyavana, where Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma washed their dusty feet before visiting their in-laws in Kāman. A third, at the base of Govardhana Hill, collected the tears of Indra, who repented his offence, and it was there that Caitanya Mahāprabhu rested during His parikrama of Govardhana.

Listed in a Vraja pastime-places catalogue as: Footprints of Kṛṣṇa (Baladeva). Source: https://vanachari.blogspot.com/2023/12/pastime-places.html

summary: A special thrones (siṁhāsanas) place in Vraja listed in a Vraja pastime-places catalogue.
body:
Lukluki-kuṇḍa is listed among the Five Special Thrones (Siṁhāsanas) in Kāmyavana, as a cave above the kuṇḍa. When Kṛṣṇa meets Rādhā here, His cowherd friends are resting at Bhojana-sthalī nearby, waiting for Him to return. Tradition presents these daytime meetings as a regular feature of the pastimes in this part of the dhāma.
