title: Gula-kuṇḍa
summary: Gula-kuṇḍa is a small lake within Dāmodaravana, in a rose garden called Gula-camana that has a grove of climbing roses.
body: Gula-kuṇḍa is a small lake within Dāmodaravana, in a rose garden called Gula-camana that has a grove of climbing roses. It was created for the pleasure of Rādhā-Dāmodara and Rādhā-Śyāmasundara. It is mentioned mainly in passing, in its description of the forest.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Gulāla-kuṇḍa
summary: Gulāla-kuṇḍa is a lake to the left of the parikrama path, near the village of Gāṅṭhuli, connected with the pastimes of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa playing Holī.
body: Gulāla-kuṇḍa is a lake to the left of the parikrama path, near the village of Gāṅṭhuli, connected with the pastimes of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa playing Holī. After the gopīs chastised Kṛṣṇa's mischievous friends with coloured powder, Kṛṣṇa and the gopīs bathed in the nearby lake to wash off the gulāla and changed into fresh clothes. At times in spring coloured dyes become visible in its waters.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Gupta-kuṇḍa
summary: Gupta-kuṇḍa is a hidden lake opposite Akrūra-sthāna where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa secretly meet early in the morning.
body: Gupta-kuṇḍa is a hidden lake opposite Akrūra-sthāna where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa secretly meet early in the morning. It is one of Vraja's three special meeting places (yoga-pīṭhas), along with Mādana-sukhadā-kuñja at Rādhā-kuṇḍa and the jewelled temple at Govinda-sthalī. The Deity Vajra installed there was defaced by soldiers in Aurangzeb's time, though locals still show Him respect.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Guñjāvana
summary: Guñjāvana is a tranquil cluster of guñjā vines downstream in Vraja, where red berries lie scattered on the ground.
body: Guñjāvana is a tranquil cluster of guñjā vines downstream in Vraja, where red berries lie scattered on the ground. Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa came here to make crowns, necklaces and bracelets solely from guñjā beads and decorated each other with them. Paurṇamāsī-devī once noticed that Śrīmatī Rādhārāṇī's heart overflowed with ecstasy at the sight of a guñjā necklace.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Guṇānandaprada-kuñja
summary: Guṇānandaprada-kuñja is the grove of the mañjarī Guṇa-mañjarī, tucked into the northern part of Campakalatā-devī's expansive grove beyond Ratyambuja-kuñja.
body: Guṇānandaprada-kuñja is the grove of the mañjarī Guṇa-mañjarī, tucked into the northern part of Campakalatā-devī's expansive grove beyond Ratyambuja-kuñja. Guṇa-mañjarī is three days junior to Tulasī-mañjarī and likes to wear red clothes resembling the japā flower. Her manners can sometimes seem brusque.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Gvāla-kuṇḍa
summary: Gvāla-kuṇḍa, also known as Gopāla-kuṇḍa, is a rarely visited and poorly maintained lake near Gvālavana.
body: Gvāla-kuṇḍa, also known as Gopāla-kuṇḍa, is a rarely visited and poorly maintained lake near Gvālavana. Gvāla means cowherd boy, and it was here that Kṛṣṇa left the gopas one morning before meeting Rādhā and Her friends at Śyāmavana. The area is a favourite resting place where the cowherd boys take lunch or a late-morning snack.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Gvālavana
summary: Gvālavana is a forest adjoining Śyāmavana and a favourite resting place for Kṛṣṇa's cowherd friends, who often take their lunch there.
body: Gvālavana is a forest adjoining Śyāmavana and a favourite resting place for Kṛṣṇa's cowherd friends, who often take their lunch there. A prasāda theft is recalled in Gvālavana in which Madhumaṅgala was the victim, after he and Kṛṣṇa had conducted the Sūrya-pūjā at Sūrya-kuṇḍa. Kṛṣṇa and His friends passed their days here playing until the calves tired and the boys went home.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Gāṅṭhuli-grāma
summary: Gāṅṭhuli-grāma is a village near the parikrama path connected with Holī pastimes and close to Gulāla-kuṇḍa.
body: Gāṅṭhuli-grāma is a village near the parikrama path connected with Holī pastimes and close to Gulāla-kuṇḍa. Fleeing Muslim soldiers, Gopāla hid in Gāṅṭhuli-grāma so that Lord Caitanya could see Him, and Caitanya Mahāprabhu stayed there three days, chanting and dancing before the Deity until day's end. Gopāla earlier escaped to Mathurā, where He favoured the Gosvāmīs for a month before returning to Govardhana Hill.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Harajī-kuṇḍa
summary: Harajī-kuṇḍa is a larger lake in which Rudra-kuṇḍa sits, at Rudravana in Bhauma Vṛndāvana.
body: Harajī-kuṇḍa is a larger lake in which Rudra-kuṇḍa sits, at Rudravana in Bhauma Vṛndāvana. It is named after the gopa Hara, who played ball with Kṛṣṇa in a nearby clearing called Gendoka-kṣetra. Vaiṣṇavas visit the secluded Rudra-kuṇḍa to pay respects to Lord Śiva as the best of all devotees of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Hari-dhāma
summary: Hari-dhāma is one of the graded abodes of the Lord, which Lord Brahmā describes in a verse as lying above Maheśa-dhāma and below Goloka, Kṛṣṇa's own realm.
body: Hari-dhāma is one of the graded abodes of the Lord, which Lord Brahmā describes in a verse as lying above Maheśa-dhāma and below Goloka, Kṛṣṇa's own realm. This verse is cited in discussions of the hierarchy of realms. It also says that Vṛṣabhānu-pura, Rādhā's home, cannot be influenced by Hari-dhāma or Devī-dhāma because of Her sweet youthfulness.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Harideva-kuṇḍa
summary: Harideva-kuṇḍa, also sometimes called Pañca-tīrtha-kuṇḍa, appears mainly in devotional accounts's notes.
body: Harideva-kuṇḍa, also sometimes called Pañca-tīrtha-kuṇḍa, appears mainly in devotional accounts's notes. The notes say Kṛṣṇa and the gopas enjoyed playing ball there, so the area is known as Kanduka-kṣetra, the ball field. Beyond that tradition says little about it.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Haritmaṇimāyā-kuñja
summary: Haritmaṇimāyā-kuñja is a grove of illusion on the southern side of Śyāma-kuṇḍa, where bees, birds, vines and cottages appear to be made of emerald (harit-maṇi).
body: Haritmaṇimāyā-kuñja is a grove of illusion on the southern side of Śyāma-kuṇḍa, where bees, birds, vines and cottages appear to be made of emerald (harit-maṇi). It is Vidagdha's pleasure grove, overseen by Campakalatā, where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa play dice (chaupaṛ) and vanish from sight as their sapphire and golden complexions blend into green. Kṛṣṇa proposed this game after His daily bath in Rādhā-kuṇḍa, with Madhu and Lalitā advising the players.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Holīvana
summary: Holīvana is a place where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa play Holī, the springtime colour festival, and it contains Alabāi (formerly Ārabāḍī), the last pastime place on the circuit around Kṛṣṇa-kuṇḍa-ṭīlā.
body: Holīvana is a place where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa play Holī, the springtime colour festival, and it contains Alabāi (formerly Ārabāḍī), the last pastime place on the circuit around Kṛṣṇa-kuṇḍa-ṭīlā. Holīvana is named with Raṇavārī and Alabāi as places that bring Holī pastimes to mind. It invites readers to sit there and chant Kṛṣṇa's holy names, hoping their hearts will turn red with the powder of the divine couple's Holī.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Hāsyavana
summary: Hāsyavana is a forest at the tip of New Vraja-dhāma's southern petal, home to Hāsanapura, the capital of the secondary mellow of humour.
body: Hāsyavana is a forest at the tip of New Vraja-dhāma's southern petal, home to Hāsanapura, the capital of the secondary mellow of humour. The sweet laughter of Kṛṣṇa and the gopas spread to the forest creatures, birds, trees and creepers until all of Hāsyavana was laughing. The echoes there still carry the gopas' laughter, which overtakes pure-hearted listeners.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Hāū-bilāū-kuṇḍa
summary: Hāū-bilāū-kuṇḍa lies near Nandīśvara Hill, close to Yaśodā-kuṇḍa and a thicket of thorn trees.
body: Hāū-bilāū-kuṇḍa lies near Nandīśvara Hill, close to Yaśodā-kuṇḍa and a thicket of thorn trees. Mother Yaśodā bathes at Yaśodā-kuṇḍa and bathes Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma there when They are awake. Devotional accounts mention Hāū-bilāū-kuṇḍa mainly in passing.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Hṛdaya-sarovara
summary: Hṛdaya-sarovara is another name for Māna-sarovara, a lake not far inland from the Yamunā famous for its sylvan beauty.
body: Hṛdaya-sarovara is another name for Māna-sarovara, a lake not far inland from the Yamunā famous for its sylvan beauty. It was born of Rādhā's tears, and Kṛṣṇa said it was like His heart, but Rādhā replied that it was her heart, so it is called the heart of both. Devotees who chant nāma-saṅkīrtana there can feel the divine couple's heartbeat.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Indra-dhvaja-sarovara
summary: Indra-dhvaja-sarovara is one of the beautiful lakes that circle Govardhana Hill, and the account names it in a verse glorifying these transcendental lakes.
body: Indra-dhvaja-sarovara is one of the beautiful lakes that circle Govardhana Hill, and the account names it in a verse glorifying these transcendental lakes. It is listed alongside Kadamba-khaṇḍa-sarovara, Sumanaḥ-sarovara and Jyotsna-mokṣaṇa-sarovara. Little more is said about it.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Indra-dhvaja-tīrtha
summary: Indra-dhvaja-tīrtha is the spot where the Vraja community used to hoist a flag in honour of Indra.
body: Indra-dhvaja-tīrtha is the spot where the Vraja community used to hoist a flag in honour of Indra. When Kṛṣṇa urged them to worship Govardhana Hill instead, the flag was not raised there, and Nanda Mahārāja put up colourful flags along the hundred peaks of Govardhana. Kṛṣṇa declared that He would end Indra's worship and introduce worship of Himself through Govardhana Hill, and the nearby Ṛṇamocana-kuṇḍa and Pāpamocana-kuṇḍa, which free bathers from all vices, have been filled in by development.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Indra-kuṇḍa
summary: Indra-kuṇḍa is a lake in Indrolī where King Indra's tears of remorse collected after Kṛṣṇa punished him for attacking the Vraja-vāsīs.
body: Indra-kuṇḍa is a lake in Indrolī where King Indra's tears of remorse collected after Kṛṣṇa punished him for attacking the Vraja-vāsīs. Contact with its water arouses real contrition for one's offences. Related places include Reheja, where Indra fell at Kṛṣṇa's feet, Indra-vedī, where he prayed, and Indra-ṭīlā, where he bathed Kṛṣṇa and named Him Govinda.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Jagannātha-ghāṭa
summary: Jagannātha-ghāṭa is a relatively recent pastime place on the Yamunā, the residence of Jagannātha, Baladeva and Subhadrā.
body: Jagannātha-ghāṭa is a relatively recent pastime place on the Yamunā, the residence of Jagannātha, Baladeva and Subhadrā. The Lord of Puruṣottama-kṣetra decided He wanted to reside in Vṛndāvana and made His own arrangements, appearing in a dream to the devotee Haridāsa, who lived and worshipped at Vaṁśīvaṭa. The forest area north of Abhirāma Ṭhākura's samādhi, extending to this ghāṭa, is called Rādhāvana, which is as dear to Rādhā as Her lake.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Jajigrāma
summary: Jajigrāma is the village to which Śrīnivāsa's family moved after his father's passing, and where his mother lived.
body: Jajigrāma is the village to which Śrīnivāsa's family moved after his father's passing, and where his mother lived. Śrīnivāsa set out for Purī to find Caitanya Mahāprabhu, but arrived after the Lord had disappeared. Later he travelled to Jajigrāma to visit his mother, and Rāmacandra, who had stayed behind at Kheturī with Narottama Dāsa, returned there looking pensive.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Jamadagni-kuṇḍa
summary: Jamadagni-kuṇḍa is one of several lakes in the village of Dakṣiṇā (also called Jakhīna), where the sage Jamadagni once resided, along with Reṇukā-kuṇḍa.
body: Jamadagni-kuṇḍa is one of several lakes in the village of Dakṣiṇā (also called Jakhīna), where the sage Jamadagni once resided, along with Reṇukā-kuṇḍa. The village's name comes from a witch (yakṣiṇī) who disturbed the area until Balarāma killed her, and nearby Balarāma-kuṇḍa and Revatī-kuṇḍa honour Him and His consort. Devotional accounts mention these lakes mainly in describing Dakṣiṇā.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Jhariwale-bābā-kuṇḍa
summary: Jhariwale-bābā-kuṇḍa is a remote lake near Varṣāṇā, on whose bank Aśvatthāmā is said to live, and it is popular with ascetics.
body: Jhariwale-bābā-kuṇḍa is a remote lake near Varṣāṇā, on whose bank Aśvatthāmā is said to live, and it is popular with ascetics. It has a rāsa-vedī on its banks commemorating the dance Kṛṣṇa performed there. Tradition passed it while walking the complete parikrama of Varṣāṇā.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Jhunakī-kuṇḍa
summary: Jhunakī-kuṇḍa is a hidden lake in Domīlavana, the forest between Nandagrāma and Saṅketa where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa meet.
body: Jhunakī-kuṇḍa is a hidden lake in Domīlavana, the forest between Nandagrāma and Saṅketa where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa meet. It and the nearby Runakī-kuṇḍa bear the names of two gopīs who arranged for the divine couple to meet there. The forest is also called Domanavana, because the minds (mana) of the couple merge there.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Jhūlana-ghāṭa
summary: Jhūlana-ghāṭa is the western shore of Rādhā-kuṇḍa, named after a banyan tree that once stood between the groves of Tuṅgavidyā and Sudevī and from which Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa enjoyed swing pastimes.
body: Jhūlana-ghāṭa is the western shore of Rādhā-kuṇḍa, named after a banyan tree that once stood between the groves of Tuṅgavidyā and Sudevī and from which Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa enjoyed swing pastimes. A humble stone frame for a swing now marks the spot.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Jhūlanavana
summary: Jhūlanavana is the open field and woods behind the Grantha-samādhi, near the samādhi of Sanātana Gosvāmī, named after the swing pastimes of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa with Their friends.
body: Jhūlanavana is the open field and woods behind the Grantha-samādhi, near the samādhi of Sanātana Gosvāmī, named after the swing pastimes of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa with Their friends. Swing pastimes evoke in Rādhā, or in any gopī who joins Kṛṣṇa on the swing, a special dependence that surpasses even her usual dependence on the Lord.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Jyotsna-mokṣaṇa-sarovara
summary: Jyotsna-mokṣaṇa-sarovara is one of the lakes circling Govardhana Hill, named in the same verse that glorifies these transcendental lakes as Indra-dhvaja-sarovara.
body: Jyotsna-mokṣaṇa-sarovara is one of the lakes circling Govardhana Hill, named in the same verse that glorifies these transcendental lakes as Indra-dhvaja-sarovara. It appears only in that list. It is mentioned mainly in passing.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Jāhnavā-ghāṭa
summary: Jāhnavā-ghāṭa is the northern shore of Rādhā-kuṇḍa, where Jāhnavā-mātā, consort of Lord Nityānanda, sat.
body: Jāhnavā-ghāṭa is the northern shore of Rādhā-kuṇḍa, where Jāhnavā-mātā, consort of Lord Nityānanda, sat. One day Kṛṣṇa appeared there in His threefold-bending form, playing His flute and gazing at her, so her private bathing stairway became known as Jāhnavā-ghāṭa. The Rādhā-Gopīnātha temple there commemorates her darśana of Gopīnātha. The account also recounts how Sanātana Gosvāmī ran along this ghāṭa warning the playing girls of a snake, and they laughed at him.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kacchapa-tīrtha
summary: Kacchapa-tīrtha, also called Kacchapavana, is a cluster of ancient trees on the Yamunā's bank where the gopas imitated turtles (kacchapa).
body: Kacchapa-tīrtha, also called Kacchapavana, is a cluster of ancient trees on the Yamunā's bank where the gopas imitated turtles (kacchapa). The boys once saw a bale of turtles basking on a sandbank at midday while their cows drank, and they played turtle games there until they were tired. They then abandoned the game and sat down for a picnic, and the account places it just beyond Rāma-ghāṭa, before Guñjāvana.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kacchapavana
summary: Kacchapavana is the same grove as Kacchapa-tīrtha, on the Yamunā's bank.
body: Kacchapavana is the same grove as Kacchapa-tīrtha, on the Yamunā's bank. The prayers of Yamunā-devī, which are recounted when passing near Kacchapavana, were offered after she was humbled by Balarāma's strength. Fearing Him, she appeared before the Lord, fell at His lotus feet and prayed for pacification.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kalpagrāma
summary: Kalpagrāma is the place where the personified holy places gathered, with Lord Varāha residing there, to ask His protection from King Sumati's son Vimati, who set out to destroy the pilgrimage places of Mathurā.
body: Kalpagrāma is the place where the personified holy places gathered, with Lord Varāha residing there, to ask His protection from King Sumati's son Vimati, who set out to destroy the pilgrimage places of Mathurā. Lord Varāha rushed to Mathurā and fought Vimati on the bank of the Yamunā, slaying him with His sword. A kuṇḍa appeared where the tip of the Lord's sword struck the ground.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kamala-kuṇḍa
summary: Kamala-kuṇḍa, also known as Kumuda-kuṇḍa, lies behind Ariṣṭa-ṭīlā beside Keli-kuṇḍa.
body: Kamala-kuṇḍa, also known as Kumuda-kuṇḍa, lies behind Ariṣṭa-ṭīlā beside Keli-kuṇḍa. Keli-kuṇḍa is where Kṛṣṇa enjoyed water-sports with His friends and, whenever possible, with Rādhā and the gopīs, and a platform there commemorates the rāsa-līlā. Ariṣṭa-ṭīlā is where the bull demon Ariṣṭāsura emerged, and Hari killed him there.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kanaka-kuñja
summary: Kanaka-kuñja is the area encircling Śyāmānanda Prabhu's puṣpa-samādhi and the Tilaka-sthāna, marking the grove where Kanaka-mañjarī resides and serves the divine couple.
body: Kanaka-kuñja is the area encircling Śyāmānanda Prabhu's puṣpa-samādhi and the Tilaka-sthāna, marking the grove where Kanaka-mañjarī resides and serves the divine couple. Śyāmānanda entered the divine couple's eternal abode as Kanaka-mañjarī at Gopīvallabha-pura, where his body was placed in samādhi and is worshipped today. Devotees offer obeisances to him for teaching how to serve the spiritual masters and for his fearless preaching of Caitanya Mahāprabhu's mission.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kanakhala-tīrtha
summary: Kanakhala-tīrtha is a secret bathing place in Mathurā that awards heavenly happiness.
body: Kanakhala-tīrtha is a secret bathing place in Mathurā that awards heavenly happiness. Vajra installed a Deity of Rameśvara there, and its ghāṭa corresponds to holy Rameśvaram. It is listed among the twenty-four bathing ghāṭas of Mathurā, which devotees should visit before circumambulating the Janmasthāna, the place of Kṛṣṇa's birth.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kanduka-tīrtha
summary: Kanduka-tīrtha is named in devotional accounts only as one of the parts of Govardhana Hill's form, where it is described as one of the hill's two sides.
body: Kanduka-tīrtha is named in devotional accounts only as one of the parts of Govardhana Hill's form, where it is described as one of the hill's two sides. Devotional accounts give no pastime for this tīrtha. The passage is presented as a description of Govardhana's transcendental body, and hearing it is said to remove sins.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kastūryānandada-kuñja
summary: Kastūryānandada-kuñja is a grove in a part of Raṅgadevī's grove where Kastūrī-mañjarī, a thirteen-year-old with a golden complexion who dresses in white crystal-coloured clothes, blissfully resides.
body: Kastūryānandada-kuñja is a grove in a part of Raṅgadevī's grove where Kastūrī-mañjarī, a thirteen-year-old with a golden complexion who dresses in white crystal-coloured clothes, blissfully resides. In Lord Caitanya's pastimes this mañjarī appears as Kṛṣṇadāsa Gosvāmī, the Lord's poetic biographer and chronicler of Kṛṣṇa's eightfold daily pastimes, who earned the title Kavirāja. He lived on the bank of Śyāma-kuṇḍa and composed his great works there.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kaṅkhala-ghāṭa
summary: Kaṅkhala-ghāṭa is a bathing place on the Yamunā in Mathurā where Vajra installed the Deity of Rameśvara, and the ghāṭa is said to correspond to holy Rameśvaram.
body: Kaṅkhala-ghāṭa is a bathing place on the Yamunā in Mathurā where Vajra installed the Deity of Rameśvara, and the ghāṭa is said to correspond to holy Rameśvaram. The place of the same name in Haridvāra is where Satī gave up her body at Dakṣa's sacrifice after hearing Lord Śiva insulted. Further downstream lies Tinduka-tīrtha, where a destitute barber named Tinduka bathed and was reborn as an aristocratic brāhmaṇa.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kaṅkhala-tīrtha
summary: Kaṅkhala-tīrtha, which the account also spells Kanakhala-tīrtha, is described as a secret place in the Mathurā area that awards heavenly happiness.
body: Kaṅkhala-tīrtha, which the account also spells Kanakhala-tīrtha, is described as a secret place in the Mathurā area that awards heavenly happiness. Vajra installed the Deity of Rameśvara there, and it corresponds to the Kaṅkhala in Haridvāra where Satī gave up her body at Dakṣa's sacrifice. Tradition notes that Tinduka-tīrtha lies further downstream.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Keli-kadamba
summary: Keli-kadamba is a kadamba tree behind the temple of Rūpa and Sanātana Gosvāmī, near Rādhā-kuṇḍa and Śyāma-kuṇḍa.
body: Keli-kadamba is a kadamba tree behind the temple of Rūpa and Sanātana Gosvāmī, near Rādhā-kuṇḍa and Śyāma-kuṇḍa. Lord Caitanya met the two brothers under this tree. Tradition notes another tree nearby under which Lord Nityānanda once sat.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Keli-kuṇḍa
summary: Keli-kuṇḍa is a lake behind Ariṣṭa-ṭīlā, the hill from which the bull demon Ariṣṭāsura emerged, and Kṛṣṇa killed him there.
body: Keli-kuṇḍa is a lake behind Ariṣṭa-ṭīlā, the hill from which the bull demon Ariṣṭāsura emerged, and Kṛṣṇa killed him there. Kṛṣṇa enjoyed water-sports (keli) with His friends and, whenever possible, with Śrī Rādhā and the gopīs. A platform on the bank commemorates the rāsa-līlā, and the Vaṁśī-vaṭa tree marks where Kṛṣṇa called the gopīs with His flute.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kevārivana
summary: Kevārivana is a pastime forest near Chattravana that shelters two temples and several samādhis, including that of Rāmānanda Rāya.
body: Kevārivana is a pastime forest near Chattravana that shelters two temples and several samādhis, including that of Rāmānanda Rāya. The forest got its name the night Kṛṣṇa defeated the hundred-hooded Kāliya and banished him to Ramaṇaka Island. Later, when a demon friend of Kaṁsa set a ring of fire around Kṛṣṇa and the Vraja-vāsīs, Kṛṣṇa swallowed the fire unseen, and the people asked, 'Who put it out?' (ke nivāri), which gave the forest its name.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Keśī-tīrtha
summary: Keśī-tīrtha is the place where Kṛṣṇa killed the demon Keśī and then bathed in the Yamunā.
body: Keśī-tīrtha is the place where Kṛṣṇa killed the demon Keśī and then bathed in the Yamunā. After the battle everyone rested at nearby Cīra-ghāṭa, which Jīva Gosvāmī says was originally called Cena-ghāṭa, and the account describes Keśī being kept tamed in a corral at Nandagrāma for the boys to ride. Keśī-tīrtha is a hundred times more sacred than the Ganges, and offering piṇḍa there gives the same result as offering it at Gayā. Tradition mentions Rāja-ghāṭa, where Rādhārāṇī and Her companions threatened to report a lazy boatman to the king, and where Lord Caitanya rested under a banyan tree.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Khelā-tīrtha
summary: Khelā-tīrtha is the same place as Khelanavana, the stretch of Yamunā riverbank where Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma play games with the cowherd boys, including ball games and mock fights.
body: Khelā-tīrtha is the same place as Khelanavana, the stretch of Yamunā riverbank where Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma play games with the cowherd boys, including ball games and mock fights. Lord Caitanya came here from Śeṣaśāyī during His visit to Vṛndāvana and then crossed the river to Bhadravana. Rūpa Gosvāmī describes it as the place where Kṛṣṇa eternally enjoys pastimes with Śrīmatī Rādhārāṇī, and the boys play all sorts of games here, completely immersing themselves in whatever they do.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kiśoravana
summary: Kiśoravana is a small forest near Sevā-kuñja where Advaita Ācārya stayed below the Advaita-vaṭa tree during His visit to Vṛndāvana.
body: Kiśoravana is a small forest near Sevā-kuñja where Advaita Ācārya stayed below the Advaita-vaṭa tree during His visit to Vṛndāvana. From there He visited Gokula, found the Deity of Madana-gopāla, and brought Him back to Kiśoravana. An account describes the Muslim king's soldiers seeking that Deity while Advaita Ācārya was away.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kiśorī-kuñja
summary: Kiśorī-kuñja is the cottage of a friend in the centre of Yāvaṭā, next to Kiśorī-kuṇḍa, where tradition sat and recalled pastimes.
body: Kiśorī-kuñja is the cottage of a friend in the centre of Yāvaṭā, next to Kiśorī-kuṇḍa, where tradition sat and recalled pastimes. On Kiśorī-kuṇḍa's southern bank is a peninsula where the sounds of Kṛṣṇa's and the gopīs' nocturnal love-sports echo across the water. Tradition also mentions the garden and the Abhimanyu house nearby, though the account does not detail their pastimes.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kiśorī-kuṇḍa
summary: Kiśorī-kuṇḍa is a lake in Yāvaṭā that commemorates Rādhā's coronation bath, and tradition says Rādhā was crowned queen of Vṛndāvana at Umrao, just south of Rahela.
body: Kiśorī-kuṇḍa is a lake in Yāvaṭā that commemorates Rādhā's coronation bath, and tradition says Rādhā was crowned queen of Vṛndāvana at Umrao, just south of Rahela. Lokanātha Gosvāmī stayed in a grove by this lake, and there Kṛṣṇa appeared holding a Deity of Himself and gave it to him as Rādhā-vinoda. The appendix describes how Lalitā pointed Kaṁsa to the lake, whose water fulfils all desires, so that he was transformed into a gopī.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Konāi-kuṇḍa
summary: Konāi-kuṇḍa takes its name from a pastime in which Kṛṣṇa, impatient because a gopī had not come, asked her in the words kyo n'āī, 'Why has She not come?' Vaiṣṇavas come to chant nāma-saṅkīrtana in the shade of the trees here, hoping to hear that gopī's answer.
body: Konāi-kuṇḍa takes its name from a pastime in which Kṛṣṇa, impatient because a gopī had not come, asked her in the words kyo n'āī, 'Why has She not come?' Vaiṣṇavas come to chant nāma-saṅkīrtana in the shade of the trees here, hoping to hear that gopī's answer. In Bhauma Vṛndāvana a temple of Śyāmasundara and Gopāla stands beside the lake, whose lapping waves seem to say kyo n'āī.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Konāivana
summary: Konāivana is the forest through which tradition passed on the way from Raṇavārī toward Sūrya-kuṇḍa.
body: Konāivana is the forest through which tradition passed on the way from Raṇavārī toward Sūrya-kuṇḍa. Konāi-kuṇḍa is named after the pastime in the nearby forest, where Kṛṣṇa asked 'kyo n'āī,' why the gopī had not come. From there tradition climbed to Kṛṣṇa-kuṇḍa-ṭīlā and reached Sūrya-kuṇḍa, the meeting place of the divine couple presided over by the sun god.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kotharā-kuṇḍa
summary: Kotharā-kuṇḍa is a lake at Kotharā in New Vraja-dhāma, where the parikrama path turns abruptly toward Kāmyavana.
body: Kotharā-kuṇḍa is a lake at Kotharā in New Vraja-dhāma, where the parikrama path turns abruptly toward Kāmyavana. It provides fresh drinking water for Kṛṣṇa's cows and a resting place for them before they return home from this far corner of the dhāma. A temple of Lord Nārāyaṇa stands there today.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kośīvana
summary: Kośīvana is the forest containing Kośīkalā, one of Nanda Mahārāja's principal granaries, which learned Vaiṣṇavas accept as Dvārakā Purī manifest in Vraja.
body: Kośīvana is the forest containing Kośīkalā, one of Nanda Mahārāja's principal granaries, which learned Vaiṣṇavas accept as Dvārakā Purī manifest in Vraja. When Nanda doubted Kṛṣṇa's claim that Kuśasthalī and the ocean were present in Vraja, Kṛṣṇa led him to Gomatī-kuṇḍa, where Nanda saw the ocean, Gomatī-ghāṭa, and Dvārakā. The forest's name comes from a joke between Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, in which She asked 'ko 'si' (who are you) when He knocked on the grove door.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Koṭavana
summary: Koṭavana is mentioned mainly in the festival calendar, where Holī is celebrated in Baṭhain and Koṭavana on the third day of the dark half of Caitra, after Vṛndāvana, Mathurā, Baladeva and Yāvaṭā.
body: Koṭavana is mentioned mainly in the festival calendar, where Holī is celebrated in Baṭhain and Koṭavana on the third day of the dark half of Caitra, after Vṛndāvana, Mathurā, Baladeva and Yāvaṭā. Devotional accounts describe no pastime at this forest. It is listed in traditional accounts's descriptions of festival dates and the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava holy days.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Koṭi-ghāṭa
summary: Koṭi-ghāṭa is a secluded bathing place on the Yamunā in Kṛṣṇa Valley, the tīrtha closest downstream from Akrūra-ghāṭa.
body: Koṭi-ghāṭa is a secluded bathing place on the Yamunā in Kṛṣṇa Valley, the tīrtha closest downstream from Akrūra-ghāṭa. A bath here gives the piety of giving millions (koṭi) of cows in charity or of taking a million baths in the Ganges. The next bathing place is Vighnarāja-ghāṭa, also called Gaṇeśa-ghāṭa.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Koṭi-tīrtha
summary: Koṭi-tīrtha is a holy place on the Yamunā, one of the twenty-four bathing places above and below Viśrāma-ghāṭa.
body: Koṭi-tīrtha is a holy place on the Yamunā, one of the twenty-four bathing places above and below Viśrāma-ghāṭa. It is named because millions (koṭi) of demigods seek to reside there and grant blessings to those who give charity or bathe nearby. It lies just downstream from Mokṣa-tīrtha, and the last of the twenty-four is Bodhi-tīrtha, said to equal Bodhgayā.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kubjā-tīrtha
summary: Kubjā-tīrtha is the home Viśvakarmā built for Kubjā on Kṛṣṇa's order, as her reward for offering Him ointments she had prepared for Kaṁsa.
body: Kubjā-tīrtha is the home Viśvakarmā built for Kubjā on Kṛṣṇa's order, as her reward for offering Him ointments she had prepared for Kaṁsa. Kṛṣṇa met and blessed her on His first evening in Mathurā, and though nearly a year passed before He visited her, He did fulfil that promise. Tradition says that on Nāga-pañcamī new brides come here to bathe in the well water and worship Kṛṣṇa for marital success and pure devotion.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kulīna-grāma
summary: Kulīna-grāma is the village where Haridāsa Ṭhākura chanted the holy names during cāturmāsya at the home of Satyarāja Khān.
body: Kulīna-grāma is the village where Haridāsa Ṭhākura chanted the holy names during cāturmāsya at the home of Satyarāja Khān. Satyarāja Khān and his son Rāmānanda Vasu, a devotee of Lord Nityānanda, both received Haridāsa's full mercy. Lord Caitanya taught the people of this village that chanting the holy name does not depend on initiation, and a first-class Vaiṣṇava is one whose presence makes others chant Kṛṣṇa's name.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kumuda-kuṇḍa
summary: Kumuda-kuṇḍa is a lake in Kumudavana, also known as Kamala-kuṇḍa, where a quarrel broke out between Kṛṣṇa's side and Balarāma's side during the boys' games with Śrīdāmā and Subala.
body: Kumuda-kuṇḍa is a lake in Kumudavana, also known as Kamala-kuṇḍa, where a quarrel broke out between Kṛṣṇa's side and Balarāma's side during the boys' games with Śrīdāmā and Subala. Caitanya Mahāprabhu was told by Kṛṣṇadāsa that the place is named Kondaliyā for this quarrel (kondala), and the Lord was pleased to hear it. On a night in Vaiśākha, Kṛṣṇa brought the gopīs here for a rāsa dance, and Rādhikā decorated Him with flowers.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kuntala-kuṇḍa
summary: Kuntala-kuṇḍa is a lake where Balarāma guided the dusty cowherd boys to bathe after their play, so that Mother Yaśodā would not be angry, and where they decorated Kṛṣṇa's hair with feathers and flowers.
body: Kuntala-kuṇḍa is a lake where Balarāma guided the dusty cowherd boys to bathe after their play, so that Mother Yaśodā would not be angry, and where they decorated Kṛṣṇa's hair with feathers and flowers. Another time Rādhā was drawn to the grove's cool shade, and her maidservants decorated her hair there. The lake is named kuntala (hair) because its waters and garden served the hair of both Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kusumavana
summary: Kusumavana is the central part of Puṣpavana, surrounded by opulent gardens and kadamba trees, and the lake there is named Kusuma-sarovara after it.
body: Kusumavana is the central part of Puṣpavana, surrounded by opulent gardens and kadamba trees, and the lake there is named Kusuma-sarovara after it. Kṛṣṇa descended to the lake's ghāṭa to gather water and sprinkle it over His basket of flowers. It is called this lake the heartbeat of Giri Govardhana because it was the site of Kṛṣṇa's intimate service to Rādhā.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kuvera-tīrtha
summary: Kuvera-tīrtha is mentioned in devotional accounts's description of Govardhana Hill's form, where it is named as the hill's determination, while Brahma-tīrtha is its cheerfulness and Yama-tīrtha its ego.
body: Kuvera-tīrtha is mentioned in devotional accounts's description of Govardhana Hill's form, where it is named as the hill's determination, while Brahma-tīrtha is its cheerfulness and Yama-tīrtha its ego. Devotional accounts give no pastime for this tīrtha. The passage says that faithful hearing of such descriptions removes all sins and makes one eligible to return to Goloka Vṛndāvana.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kuñjavana
summary: Kuñjavana is the forest that came to be called Sevā-kuñja, because Kṛṣṇa rendered the most menial service (sevā) to Śrī Rādhā in one of its groves.
body: Kuñjavana is the forest that came to be called Sevā-kuñja, because Kṛṣṇa rendered the most menial service (sevā) to Śrī Rādhā in one of its groves. The gopīs named it after that service, and in time the whole forest took that name. In the northwest corner of New Vraja-dhāma's Sevā-kuñja, a house represents Bhauma Vṛndāvana's temple of Rādhā-ramaṇa.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kuṇḍavana
summary: Kuṇḍavana is a forest near Kāmyavana, where Kṛṣṇa left His footprint on the adjacent Candrasena Hill at the junction of spring and summer while rāsa dancing with the gopīs.
body: Kuṇḍavana is a forest near Kāmyavana, where Kṛṣṇa left His footprint on the adjacent Candrasena Hill at the junction of spring and summer while rāsa dancing with the gopīs. Kṛṣṇa and the gopīs passed through its many groves before reaching Kāmyavana. From the summit of Candrasena Hill Kṛṣṇa played His flute so beautifully that the girls of Vraja and the demigoddesses above all fainted.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kālayavana
summary: Kālayavana is the subject of this entry, which tells the story of the Yavana king who laid siege to Mathurā at the same time as Jarāsandha.
body: Kālayavana is the subject of this entry, which tells the story of the Yavana king who laid siege to Mathurā at the same time as Jarāsandha. Kṛṣṇa moved the people of Mathurā to Dvārakā, which the demigods had built in the western ocean, and then faced Kālayavana unarmed. He lured the king into a cave, where Mucukunda burnt him to ashes, and then returned to destroy his army.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kāliya-ghāṭa
summary: Kāliya-ghāṭa is a bathing place on the Yamunā where the tree from which Kṛṣṇa jumped into the water to subdue Kāliya still stands beside a Deity of Kāliya-mardana installed by Vajra.
body: Kāliya-ghāṭa is a bathing place on the Yamunā where the tree from which Kṛṣṇa jumped into the water to subdue Kāliya still stands beside a Deity of Kāliya-mardana installed by Vajra. Vaiṣṇavas pray to and bathe here to be purified, and it describes how Madana-gopāla advised a merchant whose boats were stuck on the sand here to seek help from a saint. Prabodhānanda Sarasvatī's samādhi and bhajana-kuṭīra are in a courtyard behind the tree.

title: Kāliyadamana-vana
summary: Kāliyadamana-vana is the forest at the corner of Dvādaśāditya-ṭīlā that commemorates Kṛṣṇa's triumph over the hundred-headed snake Kāliya.
body: Kāliyadamana-vana is the forest at the corner of Dvādaśāditya-ṭīlā that commemorates Kṛṣṇa's triumph over the hundred-headed snake Kāliya. The house there, Nanda-bhavana, marks the samādhi of Prabodhānanda Sarasvatī Ṭhākura, and tradition notes it is not connected to Nanda Mahārāja. Behind the forest lies Gendokhara-kṣetra, where the cowherd boys played ball, and two kuṇḍas mark where Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma stood.

title: Kāma-sarovara
summary: Kāma-sarovara is a lake in Kāmyavana that resembles shimmering liquid gold, and tradition says Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa enjoy untold pastimes in its waters and surrounding gardens.
body: Kāma-sarovara is a lake in Kāmyavana that resembles shimmering liquid gold, and tradition says Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa enjoy untold pastimes in its waters and surrounding gardens. It is the foremost of the lakes in that part of Kāmyavana, which also includes Śantanu-kuṇḍa. The account also tells how Uddhava, reading Kṛṣṇa's letters, was thinking mainly of the gopīs.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kāmanā-kuṇḍa
summary: Kāmanā-kuṇḍa is a lake next to Vimala-kuṇḍa in Kāmyavana, whose water is said to be composed of kāma, the liquid essence of that forest.
body: Kāmanā-kuṇḍa is a lake next to Vimala-kuṇḍa in Kāmyavana, whose water is said to be composed of kāma, the liquid essence of that forest. A bath there can fulfil the spiritual desires of those pure in heart. The gopīs, who know the lake's secret, come there to worship and bathe with great devotion, and Kṛṣṇa appears there to reciprocate their pure kāma.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kāmaravana
summary: Kāmaravana is a forest near the summit of Govardhana Hill, and the account places it close to Phakarapura, where Kṛṣṇa made a small lake by playing His flute to quench His cowherd friends' thirst.
body: Kāmaravana is a forest near the summit of Govardhana Hill, and the account places it close to Phakarapura, where Kṛṣṇa made a small lake by playing His flute to quench His cowherd friends' thirst. Kṛṣṇa once sat on a rock here and worried, restless for Rādhā's company, when she was late because Jaṭilā was watching her closely. A stone outcrop called Caraṇa-pahāṛī, bearing Kṛṣṇa's footprints, lies further south in the district of Baiṭhana.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kāmyakavana
summary: Kāmyakavana is another name for Kāmyavana, the fourth of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, given as Kāmavana, Kāmyaka and Kāmyakavana.
body: Kāmyakavana is another name for Kāmyavana, the fourth of the twelve forests of Vṛndāvana, given as Kāmavana, Kāmyaka and Kāmyakavana. This forest fulfils all desires and is the place where Kṛṣṇa and the gopīs enjoy rāsa in its many charming groves and lakes. It also contains the village of Kāman, where Mother Yaśodā's parents lived.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kāñcana-kuṇḍa
summary: Kāñcana-kuṇḍa is the name the account gives to the lake that Vajra restored as the glorious Rādhā-kuṇḍa, while the other lake was called Vajra-kuṇḍa.
body: Kāñcana-kuṇḍa is the name the account gives to the lake that Vajra restored as the glorious Rādhā-kuṇḍa, while the other lake was called Vajra-kuṇḍa. From the night Kṛṣṇa's pastimes continued until He left for Dvārakā, the lakes of Rādhā-kuṇḍa and Śyāma-kuṇḍa were visible in their full opulence. After Kṛṣṇa left, they appeared as simple ponds until Vajra restored their glory, and tradition says Vajra named the nearby village Āriṭ-grāma.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kīlāla-kuṇḍa
summary: Kīlāla-kuṇḍa is a lake in Khelanavana where Kṛṣṇa sometimes enjoys splashing and swimming with the gopīs.
body: Kīlāla-kuṇḍa is a lake in Khelanavana where Kṛṣṇa sometimes enjoys splashing and swimming with the gopīs. At other times He and the gopas forget themselves while playing ball on its banks. The area around Nāradavana, bounded by Yugala-kuṇḍa, Khelanavana and Derāvali, is where the Vraja-vāsīs encamped during their exodus from Chaṭīkarā.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kīrti-kuṇḍa
summary: Kīrti-kuṇḍa is the bathing place of Śrī Rādhā's mother, Kīrtidā, lying east of Pīlī-pokharā under the shelter of Varṣāṇā Hill.
body: Kīrti-kuṇḍa is the bathing place of Śrī Rādhā's mother, Kīrtidā, lying east of Pīlī-pokharā under the shelter of Varṣāṇā Hill. Any creature that dies on its banks or in its waters returns to Goloka. The name Kīrtidā means one who distributes fame, like Yaśodā, and the nearby granary Bhādāvalī belonged to Nanda Mahārāja.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kīrtidā-sarovara
summary: This lake is mentioned mainly in passing, as the place also known as Kīrtidā-sarovara.
body: This lake is mentioned mainly in passing, as the place also known as Kīrtidā-sarovara. Hindus customarily bathe here at an astrologically fixed time in the winter month of Māgha, when they are said to be guaranteed liberation. The young gopīs also wanted to bathe here to observe this festival. A traditional account then cites Lord Caitanya's statement that Kṛṣṇa is an eternal youth.

title: Kṛṣṇa-gaṅgā-ghāṭa
summary: This ghāṭa lies between Vighnarāja-ghāṭa and Gokarṇa-ghāṭa in the topography of New Vraja-dhāma, downstream from Cakra-tīrtha.
body: This ghāṭa lies between Vighnarāja-ghāṭa and Gokarṇa-ghāṭa in the topography of New Vraja-dhāma, downstream from Cakra-tīrtha. It is called Kṛṣṇa-gaṅgā-ghāṭa because Kṛṣṇa made the Ganges appear in the middle of the Yamunā here. Tradition says bathing here is ten times more auspicious than the world's five most sacred baths. An island in front of the ghāṭa is also linked to the birth of Vyāsa, though that part of the account is cut short.

title: Kṛṣṇa-kuṇḍa
summary: Kṛṣṇa-kuṇḍa is another name for Madhu-kuṇḍa, in the area of the ancient city of Maholī in Madhuvana.
body: Kṛṣṇa-kuṇḍa is another name for Madhu-kuṇḍa, in the area of the ancient city of Maholī in Madhuvana. The best-known pastime here is a quarrel: Kṛṣṇa was late for a meeting with Rādhārāṇī, and she sulked in a grove of Bahulāvana. The gopīs searched for her and found her on the bank of Kṛṣṇa-kuṇḍa, and with their help Kṛṣṇa won her back. The lake has since also been called Māna-sarovara, and traditional accounts include verses praising its groves and fragrance.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Kṛṣṇavana
summary: Kṛṣṇavana is the name that covers Kṛṣṇa's seven forests in Vraja-maṇḍala, just as Bhadravana names the five forests of Balabhadra.
body: Kṛṣṇavana is the name that covers Kṛṣṇa's seven forests in Vraja-maṇḍala, just as Bhadravana names the five forests of Balabhadra. It is mentioned in passing, in a note on how the forests are named. In New Vraja-dhāma, Bhadravana is mostly fertile farmland growing wheat, mustard, and oats.

title: Laghmohana-kuṇḍa
summary: In the prayer from Vilāpa-kusumāñjali, Raghunātha Dāsa Gosvāmī recalls living at Laghmohana-kuṇḍa until Sanātana Gosvāmī told him to move to Ariṣṭa-kuṇḍa and promised that he would receive Rādhikā's grace.
body: In the prayer from Vilāpa-kusumāñjali, Raghunātha Dāsa Gosvāmī recalls living at Laghmohana-kuṇḍa until Sanātana Gosvāmī told him to move to Ariṣṭa-kuṇḍa and promised that he would receive Rādhikā's grace. There he excavated Rādhā's lake, planted gardens around it, built cottages for sādhus on its shores, and served them daily. He also bathed in Rādhā's lake three times a day and bowed down in the prescribed manner around it.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Lagmohana-kuṇḍa
summary: This small lake, now largely hidden by buildings, lay south of the corner of Śyāma-kuṇḍa, and Raghunātha Dāsa Gosvāmī lived beside it until Sanātana Gosvāmī persuaded him to move to Rādhā-kuṇḍa.
body: This small lake, now largely hidden by buildings, lay south of the corner of Śyāma-kuṇḍa, and Raghunātha Dāsa Gosvāmī lived beside it until Sanātana Gosvāmī persuaded him to move to Rādhā-kuṇḍa. Kṛṣṇa killed the demon Śaṅkhacūḍa here at the end of a long battle that began in Śyāmavana on the night of Holī, after the demon tried to abduct Rādhārāṇī and the gopīs. Kṛṣṇa beheaded him and took the Syamantaka jewel from his crown. Because Śaṅkhacūḍa's remains scattered here, crops do not grow in the area, though trees do grow at the kuṇḍa, which is a meeting place of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Lalitā-grāma
summary: Lalitā-grāma is another name for Ūñchagaon, the village where Rādhā's best friend, Lalitā-devī, grew up.
body: Lalitā-grāma is another name for Ūñchagaon, the village where Rādhā's best friend, Lalitā-devī, grew up. Many pastimes took place there, including the marriage of Lalitā-devī and Śrī Kṛṣṇa. About three hundred years ago Varṣāṇā was only a small settlement connected to Ūñchagaon, which later flourished while Ūñchagaon fell into obscurity.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Lalitā-vivāha-sthala
summary: This hill, now called Lalitā-vivāha-sthala, is where Lalitā, who had been angry at those who conspired against her, finally relented after Rādhārāṇī embraced her.
body: This hill, now called Lalitā-vivāha-sthala, is where Lalitā, who had been angry at those who conspired against her, finally relented after Rādhārāṇī embraced her. She submitted to the will of Śrī Rādhā and joined the other gopīs in a grand wedding festival held on the hill. At Ūñchagaon one also finds Lalitā's ancestral home, where she lived with her parents until her marriage to Bhairava-gopa in Yāvaṭā-grāma.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Lalitānandada-kuñja
summary: This is Lalitā-devī's grove, located on the northern ghāṭa of Rādhā-kuṇḍa, and it is the most famous of the sakhīs' kuñjas.
body: This is Lalitā-devī's grove, located on the northern ghāṭa of Rādhā-kuṇḍa, and it is the most famous of the sakhīs' kuñjas. It is laid out as a lotus, whose innermost whorl has eight petals forming the eight principal sub-groves that are the residences and service areas of Lalitā's eight main gopī assistants. Each of those sub-groves has its own eight subordinate groves. The southern petal, Aruṇāmbuja-kuñja, is the red lotus petal of Lalitā's grove, and the southwestern petal holds a lotus temple with sixteen main chambers.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Laukika-tīrtha
summary: In one passage that assigns holy sites to the parts of a body, Laukika-tīrtha is the belly.
body: In one passage that assigns holy sites to the parts of a body, Laukika-tīrtha is the belly. In a prayer, tradition asks that he may someday hide behind a bush at this all-purifying forest garden and watch Kṛṣṇa and His friends play hide-and-seek. The passage is otherwise concerned with the devotional value of the sites rather than with a detailed pastime.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Lavaṅga-sukhada-kuñja
summary: This is the beautiful residence of Lavaṅga-mañjarī, in the eastern portion of Tuṅgavidyā's crimson-coloured grove, and it enchants the gopīs who visit.
body: This is the beautiful residence of Lavaṅga-mañjarī, in the eastern portion of Tuṅgavidyā's crimson-coloured grove, and it enchants the gopīs who visit. Lavaṅga-mañjarī is known in Vṛndāvana for her pleasing nature and beauty, with a smooth golden complexion and clothes resembling a starlit night. The account also tells of Mother Yaśodā, who, pleased by the girls' love for Rādhā, sent rice and vegetables to Rādhā and her friends.

title: Laṅkā-kuṇḍa
summary: Laṅkā-kuṇḍa, also called Setubandha-kuṇḍa, represents the point of the ocean at Rameśvara from where Lord Rāmacandra crossed to Laṅkā over a bridge of joined boulders.
body: Laṅkā-kuṇḍa, also called Setubandha-kuṇḍa, represents the point of the ocean at Rameśvara from where Lord Rāmacandra crossed to Laṅkā over a bridge of joined boulders. It lies in Kāmyavana, which tradition says is the most opulent in lakes of all the Vraja forests. One summer day Kṛṣṇa sat on its bank with Rādhārāṇī and her friends, watching monkeys leap from the trees into the water and frolic as the gopas would.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Laṛilī-kuṇḍa
summary: Laṛilī-kuṇḍa is one of the pastime places in and around Yāvaṭā.
body: Laṛilī-kuṇḍa is one of the pastime places in and around Yāvaṭā. There Lalitā arranged a meeting between Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa after two nights when Kṛṣṇa had hidden in trees. Nearby is Muktā-kuṇḍa, where the gopīs dressed Rādhā with pearl necklaces, bracelets, and a headdress before she went to meet Kṛṣṇa and freed Him from loneliness.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Leovaṭa-kuṇḍa
summary: Leovaṭa-kuṇḍa is a small lake further in the direction of Pāvana-sarovara.
body: Leovaṭa-kuṇḍa is a small lake further in the direction of Pāvana-sarovara. Here the cowherd boys enjoyed drinking buttermilk in the shade of a large banyan tree (vaṭa). Mother Yaśodā made butter by churning yogurt and fed her sons the leftover buttermilk, sweetened or salty depending on the season, a drink that cools the body in summer.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Lohajaṅghavana
summary: Lohajaṅghavana is a beautiful place full of flowering mādhavī vines, whose blossoms Kṛṣṇa used to decorate the cowherd girls' hair.
body: Lohajaṅghavana is a beautiful place full of flowering mādhavī vines, whose blossoms Kṛṣṇa used to decorate the cowherd girls' hair. Tradition places Kṛṣṇa here with Rādhārāṇī, walking along the Yamunā's shore, which was pleasant with humming bees and soft, fragrant spring breezes. This happens around the time Kaṁsa and Śaṅkhacūḍa decided to join forces against Kṛṣṇa.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Loṭana-kuṇḍa
summary: Loṭana-kuṇḍa is a lake with wide sandy banks in open pastures beyond the sandalwood forest of Candanavana, and Kṛṣṇa used to graze His herd there.
body: Loṭana-kuṇḍa is a lake with wide sandy banks in open pastures beyond the sandalwood forest of Candanavana, and Kṛṣṇa used to graze His herd there. On a hot day the cows playfully rolled (loṭ) in the cool sand, and the gopas gathered, cheered, and urged them on, until the boys rolled in the sand with the cows as well. The grazing route runs from Loṭana-kuṇḍa on to the field called Kerala.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Luklukāna-micalī-kuṇḍa
summary: This sacred lake lies in a dense wood in Kāmyavana, reached after the parikrama path passes Laṅkā's shore and the nearby Aśokavana.
body: This sacred lake lies in a dense wood in Kāmyavana, reached after the parikrama path passes Laṅkā's shore and the nearby Aśokavana. Kṛṣṇa and the cowherd girls play hide-and-seek in and around the lake. When the gopīs are in Kāmyavana at the same time as Kṛṣṇa, they send Him a message, and once His friends doze off after their meal, He slips away to meet them here.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Lāṭhāvana
summary: Ḍīg is a large place outside Vraja-dhāma with no special religious significance and no recorded pastimes, but it is known as Lāṭhāvana.
body: Ḍīg is a large place outside Vraja-dhāma with no special religious significance and no recorded pastimes, but it is known as Lāṭhāvana. A king of Ḍīg, possibly Jawahar Singh, lamented that pilgrims did not visit his town, so he decreed that those who skipped Ḍīg would be forcibly brought there by soldiers with canes (lāṭhīs). The Skanda Purāṇa mentions the town as Dīrghapura, which Vajra was asked to repopulate.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Līlānandaprada-kuñja
summary: This is the grove of Sudevī, reached toward the end of the parikrama of Rādhā-kuṇḍa, and it is the abode of Mañjulālī-mañjarī, also called Līlā-mañjarī.
body: This is the grove of Sudevī, reached toward the end of the parikrama of Rādhā-kuṇḍa, and it is the abode of Mañjulālī-mañjarī, also called Līlā-mañjarī. She is described as thirteen and a half years old with a complexion like molten gold, and she wears reddish clothes as Rādhā sometimes does. She serves Rādhā with her expert skill at dressing and ornamenting her.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Līlāvatī-kuṇḍa
summary: Līlāvatī-kuṇḍa lies in the Sakhīvana woods beside the parikrama path near Govardhana town, together with the village Sakhī-sthalī and Sakhī-kuṇḍa.
body: Līlāvatī-kuṇḍa lies in the Sakhīvana woods beside the parikrama path near Govardhana town, together with the village Sakhī-sthalī and Sakhī-kuṇḍa. Govardhana Malla, a revenue collector for Kaṁsa, lives there with his wife Candrāvalī, whom the scriptures declare to be Kṛṣṇa's second-favourite gopī. It is said that Candrāvalī's sixty-four main girlfriends excavated the lake, and Uddhava would sit by its banks describing Kṛṣṇa's pastimes to the gopīs.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Madana-gopāla-tīrtha
summary: This forest is named for an amorous pastime of Kṛṣṇa, which Kṛṣṇadāsa narrated to Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu in a dense grove.
body: This forest is named for an amorous pastime of Kṛṣṇa, which Kṛṣṇadāsa narrated to Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu in a dense grove. Once Śrīmatī Rādhārāṇī took a circuitous route through Khadiravana, on the pretext of selling yogurt at the Nandagrāma market, in order to meet Kṛṣṇa. Tradition says Caitanya Mahāprabhu repeatedly asked to hear more of these pastimes.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Madana-mohana-ghāṭa
summary: Walking west one arrives at Madana-mohana-ghāṭa, where Sanātana Gosvāmī absorbed himself in bhajana at his sitting place on the bank of Rādhā-kuṇḍa.
body: Walking west one arrives at Madana-mohana-ghāṭa, where Sanātana Gosvāmī absorbed himself in bhajana at his sitting place on the bank of Rādhā-kuṇḍa. A Madana-mohana temple now stands there, worshipping pratibhū-mūrtis of the original Deities, who rested here on their way from Vṛndāvana town toward Karoli. The surrounding passage also tells of Kṛṣṇa's playful dice game, in which Rādhā claimed victory.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Madanānandada-kuñja
summary: This grove belongs to Viśākhā-devī and lies next to Lalitā's grove.
body: This grove belongs to Viśākhā-devī and lies next to Lalitā's grove. It is called Madanānandada-kuñja or Viśākhānandada-kuñja because it is said to give Cupid bliss. At its centre is a jewel-laden lotus temple with sixteen petals, furnished with beds, canopies, and curios, and surrounded by four gates of flowering vines. A verse describes how Raghunātha Dāsa Gosvāmī longs to prepare a flower bed for Rādhā in this grove.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Madhu-kuṇḍa
summary: Madhu-kuṇḍa lies in Madhuvana, where bees and beehives drip honey, and Kṛṣṇa, who always thirsts for sweetness, drinks the honey that servant boys collected for Him.
body: Madhu-kuṇḍa lies in Madhuvana, where bees and beehives drip honey, and Kṛṣṇa, who always thirsts for sweetness, drinks the honey that servant boys collected for Him. At noon the cowherd boys brought the cows to drink at its bank, and Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma sat in a flowering grove and sported together. Balarāma once visited from Dvārakā and, while narrating Kṛṣṇa's pastimes, became so absorbed in Kṛṣṇa that His body turned cloud blue, which is why the Deity of Balarāma at Madhu-kuṇḍa is blackish.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places
coordinate_source: Google Maps saved places export (via holy_places.xlsx)

title: Madhumaṅgalānandada-kuñja
summary: This is the comic grove of Madhumaṅgala, the risible brāhmaṇa jester, found on the northern side of Śyāma-kuṇḍa, and its patron is Lalitā-devī.
body: This is the comic grove of Madhumaṅgala, the risible brāhmaṇa jester, found on the northern side of Śyāma-kuṇḍa, and its patron is Lalitā-devī. Here Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, provoked by Madhu, entertain their companions and deepen their amorous feelings by exchanging jokes and speaking in riddles. The foliage, animals, and structures of the grove reflect the mellows of comedy.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Madhusūdana-kuṇḍa
summary: Madhusūdana-kuṇḍa lies on Nandīśvara Hill, beside Madhusūdanavana, and Kṛṣṇa sits alone in the shade of a bakula tree overlooking it.
body: Madhusūdana-kuṇḍa lies on Nandīśvara Hill, beside Madhusūdanavana, and Kṛṣṇa sits alone in the shade of a bakula tree overlooking it. The bees humming around the lake are described as great devotees, intoxicated by the nectar of nāma-saṅkīrtana, who sing of His pastimes of pure love. Halfway up the hill from the lake is the cave where Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu found the deities later installed on Nandīśvara Hill.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Madhusūdanavana
summary: Madhusūdanavana is a garden of diverse flowering trees and vines that runs along the length and height of Nandīśvara Hill, after the place called Gendokhara.
body: Madhusūdanavana is a garden of diverse flowering trees and vines that runs along the length and height of Nandīśvara Hill, after the place called Gendokhara. It is famous for its humming bees (madhukara). Kṛṣṇa sits here alone under a bakula tree listening to the bees, which are devotees singing of His pastimes.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Maheśa-dhāma
summary: Maheśa-dhāma is the abode of Lord Śiva (Maheśa).
body: Maheśa-dhāma is the abode of Lord Śiva (Maheśa). Lord Brahmā is quoted describing a hierarchy of realms: the mundane world (Devī-dhāma) at the bottom, then Maheśa-dhāma, then Hari-dhāma, and above them all Goloka, Kṛṣṇa's own realm. Its purpose is to glorify Goloka Vṛndāvana and its earthly counterparts, which is why it places Maheśa-dhāma below them.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Mahā-dadhi-kuṇḍa
summary: Also called Kṣīra-sāgara, this lake formed when Kṛṣṇa played His flute at Rādhā's request to show her His form resting on Śeṣa-nāga in the ocean of milk, and His cows soaked the ground with unending streams of milk.
body: Also called Kṣīra-sāgara, this lake formed when Kṛṣṇa played His flute at Rādhā's request to show her His form resting on Śeṣa-nāga in the ocean of milk, and His cows soaked the ground with unending streams of milk. In this milk-ocean appeared the serpent Śeṣa, and as Kṛṣṇa walked hand in hand with Rādhā along his body, He appeared as four-armed Viṣṇu and she as four-armed Lakṣmī.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Mahā-Vṛndāvana
summary: Mahā-Vṛndāvana is the great forest in the unmanifest realm of Goloka in the spiritual sky, and it is also known as Gokula.
body: Mahā-Vṛndāvana is the great forest in the unmanifest realm of Goloka in the spiritual sky, and it is also known as Gokula. It looks like a thousand-petalled lotus, whose hexagonal whorl is Kṛṣṇa's personal abode, while some petals are residences of the cowherd men and others are gardens of Śrī Rādhā and her gopī friends. Its many sub-forests, called Keli-Vṛndāvanas, are the settings for Kṛṣṇa's confidential pastimes.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Mahādbhuta-rāsasthala
summary: This is the fourth sub-petal of the Yoga-pīṭha, which is named for a pastime and has the same importance as the Yoga-pīṭha's inner core because Govardhana Hill is so dear to Kṛṣṇa.
body: This is the fourth sub-petal of the Yoga-pīṭha, which is named for a pastime and has the same importance as the Yoga-pīṭha's inner core because Govardhana Hill is so dear to Kṛṣṇa. Here Kṛṣṇa meets billions of gopīs for a great festival of dancing, expanding into as many forms as there are cowherd damsels to amaze them. There is another Yoga-pīṭha on Govardhana at Rādhā-kuṇḍa.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Malla-tīrtha
summary: Malla-tīrtha is the place where Kṛṣṇa honed His wrestling skills with Balarāma and the cowherd boys.
body: Malla-tīrtha is the place where Kṛṣṇa honed His wrestling skills with Balarāma and the cowherd boys. The boys locked arms and competed for the parcel of sweets they had brought, while the elder gopīs watched, amused. Gopīśvara Mahādeva, the worshipable deity of the elder gopīs, presides over the area, and nearby is a deity called Mahā-malla-rāya.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places

title: Mathurā-dhāma
summary: Mathurā-dhāma is the eternal abode of the Lord, and traditional accounts describe Prayāga-tīrtha, the third ghāṭa downstream from Viśrāma-ghāṭa, where personified Prayāga did penance for slighting it.
body: Mathurā-dhāma is the eternal abode of the Lord, and traditional accounts describe Prayāga-tīrtha, the third ghāṭa downstream from Viśrāma-ghāṭa, where personified Prayāga did penance for slighting it. Although Prayāga is called Tīrtharāja, the king of holy places, he has no authority over Mathurā-Vṛndāvana, which is not merely a tīrtha but the dhāma and not different from Kṛṣṇa Himself. The bathing place Guhya-tīrtha is said to reveal the secret of the Vedas, which is to know Kṛṣṇa.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places
coordinate_source: Google Maps saved places export (via holy_places.xlsx)

title: Mathurā-Vṛndāvana
summary: Devotional accounts quote the Skanda Purāṇa saying that the Lord ordered Arjuna to settle His queens in Vraja, which shows that Kṛṣṇa wanted them taken to Mathurā-Vṛndāvana.
body: Devotional accounts quote the Skanda Purāṇa saying that the Lord ordered Arjuna to settle His queens in Vraja, which shows that Kṛṣṇa wanted them taken to Mathurā-Vṛndāvana. After Kṛṣṇa's departure from the world, Arjuna reported this to his brothers. The account also notes that the sun-god deity at Vaṭasvāmī-tīrtha dates back to Satya-yuga, which confirms that Mathurā-Vṛndāvana has been the chief place of worship in all four ages.
source_ref: User-provided notes on Vraja holy places
